title: AI search and SQL functions in data platforms

opening.headline: If the data is already in the warehouse, AI can be used in place without taking the data out. Distinguish between the uses of SQL functions and search services.
body: Let's say you have hundreds of thousands of customer inquiries sitting on warehouse tables. To send this to the model, you need to pull out the data, call it into a separate script, and reload the results. Meanwhile, the burden of data movement, permission management, and pipeline maintenance increases.

In this lesson, we will look at the flow of Snowflake's AI functions calling models with a single line of SQL, four core functions, the Cortex Search service and dynamic tables that combine vectors and keywords, and a comparison with similar features in Databricks. Next, we will explain why the bulk row classification task is suitable for the functional type and the criteria for distinguishing between functional AI and service-type search.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the role of Snowflake AI functions and Cortex Search
The uses of functional AI and service-based search can be distinguished.
Can explain what the cost of an AI function is proportional to and how the output may vary

screens.title: The data is already in the warehouse
screens.lead: Read about situations where you want to connect data accumulated in a warehouse to a model. It is a good idea to read it while thinking about the burden that occurs along the path that data travels.

visual.alt: A path to copy data out of the warehouse table, send it to the model, and reload the results.
labels: Warehouse tables (hundreds of thousands of customer inquiries)

paragraphs: Hundreds of thousands of customer inquiries are sitting on tables in the warehouse. I would like to use a model to classify or summarize these inquiries.

A common method is to pull the data out of the warehouse, call the model in a separate script, and load the results back into the warehouse. You must create and operate the three steps yourself: extract, call, and load.

This path comes with its challenges. Data moves out of the warehouse, its permissions must be managed separately, and pipelines must be maintained. Can't we call the model right from where the data is? This class starts from that question.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Which will last longer: the cost of moving the data or the cost of calling the model? Please answer again at the end of class.

screens.outro: Before we look at how to shorten this path to SQL functions, let's first recall your experience.

screens.title: think about it
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever experienced an analyst handling data using SQL but then moving on to a separate tool for text classification?
items.answer: SQL is strong at dealing with numbers and categories, but has difficulty dealing with the meaning of sentences. So tasks like classification were often transferred to Python scripts or external tools. The AI ​​function imports this boundary into SQL.

items.prompt: Have you ever needed security clearance to export your data?
items.answer: Any data that leaves the organization's boundaries is subject to approval and auditing. Processing the data where it resides reduces this burden by allowing it to follow existing permissions mechanisms.

items.prompt: Are document retrieval and row-level conversion the same type of task or different tasks?
items.answer: It's a different task. Row-level transformation applies the same processing to all rows, and document search selects the fragment that matches the query. The former is divided into functional type and the latter is divided into service type, which is the central division of this class.

screens.outro: I will organize it into two categories: function type and service type. First, let’s look at how functional AI works.

screens.title: Flow where a single line of SQL calls a model
screens.lead: Below is an example SQL that summarizes each row from the statement table into a model. Read the explanation on the right to see how a single line of SQL calls the model.

data.code:
SELECT
  inquiry_id,
  inquiry_text,
  AI_COMPLETE(
    'model_name',
    'Summarize the following customer inquiry in one sentence:' || inquiry_text
  ) AS summary
FROM customer_inquiries
LIMIT 100;

notes.note: It looks like a regular SELECT. Change the column names or table names to suit your warehouse. There are no separate steps to retrieve the data.

Apply a prompt to each row in the form `AI_COMPLETE(model, prompt)`. The first argument is the model to use, and the second argument is the prompt. Each line is followed by a prompt and the model is called. Models must use a name that appears on the regional availability list.
The model's responses are appended to a new column called `summary`. Export the results as a separate file so you don't have to reload them.
First, try reducing the number of rows with `LIMIT`. The model is called for every row, so running hundreds of thousands of rows at once is expensive and time consuming.

A typical scalar AI function checks the account's USE AI FUNCTIONS or USE AI FUNCTION permissions on the function, along with the appropriate database role. AI_FUNCTIONS_USER is for scalar functions, aggregate functions are viewed separately. The current official guidance specifies an exception where AI_AGG·AI_SUMMARIZE_AGG can be used without CORTEX_USER if USE AI FUNCTIONS is present.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen the general purpose functions, let's distinguish four key functions.

screens.title: AI_COMPLETE, AI_FILTER, AI_AGG, AI_CLASSIFY
screens.lead: Select each tab to check the input and return values of the four functions. Even within the same SQL, pay attention to how the result shape is different for each function and how the cost is proportional to what.

tabs.label: AI_COMPLETE
tabs.body: `AI_COMPLETE(model, prompt)` is a basic, general-purpose function that generates a response to text or images. You can add model_parameters (temperature, top_p, guardrails, etc.), response_format, and show_details as optional arguments, and the default return value is the response string. Tasks that do not have a defined function, such as summarization, translation, or extraction, are handled by writing a prompt to this function. It is the most flexible, but results depend on the quality of the prompts.

tabs.label: AI_CLASSIFY
tabs.body: `AI_CLASSIFY(input, category list)` classifies the input into the specified categories, and the result is an object with a labels field. There must be at least two categories and are case sensitive; accuracy may decrease if there are more than 20 categories. Input that cannot be processed returns NULL by default. It is suitable for dividing into defined categories such as refunds, delivery, quality, and others.

tabs.label: AI_FILTER
tabs.body: `AI_FILTER(input)` returns true or false, and unprocessed input returns NULL by default. You can filter by natural language conditions in SELECT, WHERE, and JOIN ON. Conditions that are difficult to express with keywords, such as “Is this an inquiry expressing dissatisfaction?” can be used in SQL.

tabs.label: AI_AGG
tabs.body: `AI_AGG(expr, instruction)` aggregates multiple rows of a text column into one result string according to the directive. Datasets larger than the context window are also supported, allowing tens of thousands of inquiries to be summarized in a single instruction. Unlike other functions that return results per row, multiple rows are gathered into one.

tabs.label: Common
tabs.body: AI_COMPLETE·AI_CLASSIFY·AI_FILTER are scalar functions and AI_AGG is an aggregate function for text columns. Check regional availability and permission conditions for each function. Even aggregate functions are not subject to the same database role rules.

tabs.label: Stability of costs and results
tabs.body:
Snowflake documentation explains that Cortex AI functions spend credits based on token usage, and AI_COMPLETE, AI_CLASSIFY, AI_FILTER, and AI_AGG that generate text are charged for both input and output tokens. The category name, description, and example of AI_CLASSIFY are also added to the input token for each row. So the cost is roughly proportional to the number of rows and the number of tokens per row. The unit price varies depending on the model, so it is calculated according to the provider's rate table.

Three practices emerge from this structure: First, for very long columns, cut only the necessary sections. Second, look at your token and credit usage in a few rows to estimate the overall cost before turning the whole thing around. The documentation walks you through a history view that shows usage by query and a function that counts tokens. Third, when automatically updating the results of an AI function with a dynamic table, model call costs may be incurred again with each update, so do not set the target delay shorter than necessary.

The output of a generative model can vary slightly from run to run even with the same input. AI_CLASSIFY, which selects from a list of defined categories, is stable in post-processing because the result type is limited to one label, but inquiries with ambiguous boundaries may be classified differently for each execution. For important decisions, save the results in a table and reuse them.

screens.outro: Let's continue with service-type search, which contrasts with functional-type.

ext.title: Snowflake documentation: Cost considerations for Cortex AI Functions

screens.title: Cortex Search service and dynamic tables
screens.lead: Let's take a step-by-step look at how the search service is configured and updated. Select the right arrow and follow the steps from changing the original to updating the search index.

visual.alt: An update flow in which source table changes are propagated to dynamic tables and search indexes in turn.
labels: Dynamic table (defined by query, automatically updated according to TARGET_LAG)

steps.title: 1. Configure hybrid search in minutes
steps.body: Cortex Search constructs hybrid vector and keyword searches on text data in minutes. You don't have to create embeddings, manage infrastructure, tune search quality, or update indexes yourself.

steps.title: 2. Main use
steps.body: Its main uses are the RAG engine in LLM chatbots, enterprise search in app search boxes, and agents that use unstructured data. It's all about quickly finding relevant document fragments at the moment a user makes a query.

steps.title: 3. Service creation and query
steps.body: The statement that creates the service includes items such as `WAREHOUSE` and `TARGET_LAG`, and the warehouse is used to run the original query, create a search index, and update it according to the delay target. When querying, you can filter results based on the ATTRIBUTES column with `filter`, allowing you to narrow your search by department or authority.

steps.title: 4. Dynamic table
steps.body: Dynamic tables automatically update tables defined by queries according to the delay target (TARGET_LAG), which is at least 60 seconds. When the source changes, the resulting table follows within a certain delay. There is no need to run the update task manually every time.

steps.title: 5. Spread of renewal
steps.body: When the original table changes, the dynamic table is updated, and the index of the search service based on that table is also updated accordingly. Users always search for data from a similar point in time.

screens.outro: Let's compare it to similar features on external platforms.

screens.title: Comparison of Foundation Model API with other platforms
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare how Snowflake and Databricks provide the same functionality.

states.label: Snowflake
states.body: Snowflake provides AI capabilities as SQL functions and services. The functional type calls a function such as AI_COMPLETE within the query, and the service type creates a Cortex Search service and queries it. Since the user side works mainly on SQL, it is easy for analysts to access. The documentation explains that the models provided are deployed within the Snowflake service boundary, and calls require permission. Since the data and model are in the same platform, there are no separate steps to retrieve the data and send it externally.

states.label: Databricks
states.body: Databricks provides model serving endpoints and search indexes. Foundation Model APIs can be called in most OpenAI compatible ways. There are two ways to use it: pay-per-token and provisioned throughput. Pay-as-you-go is an easy way to get started, and provisioned throughput is recommended for all production workloads, especially when you need high throughput, guaranteed performance, and fine-tuned models. Databricks AI Search creates indexes from source tables, such as Delta Lake tables, and provides hybrid keyword-similarity search and filters. In summary, the differences between Snowflake and Databricks are in the form of SQL functions and services, and Databricks in the form of model serving endpoints and search indexes, but they are the same in that they provide two functions: model call and search. When moving between platforms, you need to check your code because the calling method and query form change.

screens.outro: Now that we've looked at all the functions, let's use examples to explain tasks for which the functional type is suitable.

screens.title: Explanation: Why bulk row sorting tasks are suitable for functional types
screens.lead: The instructor solves the task of classifying 500,000 customer inquiries using SQL. Select the right arrow to follow the process as each line of SQL and result table is added step by step.

visual.alt: Example of a result table with a classification column attached to the input table followed by dynamic tables, filters, and aggregations.
labels: Dynamic tables: updated according to target delay

steps.title: 1. Work definition
steps.body: We classify 500,000 customer inquiries into categories such as refunds, delivery, and quality. This is a bulk row conversion task that applies the same processing to each inquiry.

steps.title: 2. Break down SQL into one line
steps.body: Add a classification column by putting `AI_CLASSIFY(inquiry_text, ['Refund','Delivery','Quality','Other'])` in the SELECT. The result is an object with a labels field, so you can pull its values ​​out and write them into columns if needed. Categories are case-sensitive and accuracy may decrease if there are more than 20, so keep them in decimal numbers as in this example.

steps.title: 3. Do not take out data
steps.body: Because data is processed within the warehouse rather than taken out, authority and auditing follow existing systems. The three steps of extracting, calling, and loading have been reduced to one query. At first, run only some rows with LIMIT to check the classification quality.

steps.title: 4. Results into dynamic table
steps.body: By defining classification queries as dynamic tables, classification follows the target delay as new inquiries accumulate. There is no need to create and schedule separate batch jobs. However, since model call costs may arise again with each update, check token usage with a small number of rows before running the full 500,000 and set the target delay as short as necessary.

steps.title: 5. Next, filter and aggregate
steps.body: Filter out only the inquiries that express dissatisfaction with `AI_FILTER`, and obtain a summary of the complaint with `AI_AGG`. Sorting, filtering, and aggregation all occur within the same SQL.

steps.title: 6. Why functional form is right
steps.body: This is because the same processing is applied to all rows, the results are required as new columns or aggregate values, and it is a task that can be processed in batches rather than an immediate response. When these conditions are met, functional AI is the simplest choice.

screens.outro: Let’s compare this with the case where the service type is appropriate.

ext.title: Snowflake documentation: Cost considerations for Cortex AI Functions

screens.title: Explanation: Distinguishing between functional AI and service-based search
screens.lead: The instructor compares the two methods based on four criteria: units of input, timing of execution, output, and appropriate tasks. Select the right arrow to fill out the rows of the comparison table one by one.

visual.alt: A two-column table comparing functional AI and search-as-a-service based on four criteria.
labels: Search for document fragments matching a query

steps.title: input unit
steps.body: Functional types convert row by row. Every row is input and all rows are processed the same way. The service type finds document fragments that match the query. Only a portion of the entire document is selected and returned.

steps.title: When to run
steps.body: Functional types are executed in batches when queries are run. It is suitable for work where it is okay to take time to get results. As-a-Service runs with low latency when users make queries. It fits the screen where people are waiting.

steps.title: result
steps.body: The result of a functional form is a new column or aggregate value. The result of the service type is the top N document fragments that match the query, and the number is set to limit. The former results are stored and used in a table, and the later results are used in prompts or screens.

steps.title: suitable job
steps.body: Classification, extraction, and summary aggregation are functional types. The chatbot's RAG and the app's search box are service-type. Even with the same inquiry data, “divide all inquiries by type” is a functional type, and “find past inquiries similar to this question” is a service type.

steps.title: combine
steps.body: The two can be combined. For example, extract attributes such as the type of inquiry in a functional form and use those attributes as filter columns (ATTRIBUTES) for service-type search. You can then narrow it down by searching for “refund types only.”

steps.title: With authority too
steps.body: Either way requires permission. The AI ​​function checks account permissions and database role conditions for each function, and the search service can divide the access range using filters when querying. Choosing features and designing permissions should go hand in hand.

screens.outro: Now let's summarize the entire lesson.

screens.title: Where the data is, in a way that suits the job
screens.lead: Let's go back to the first question and try to tie the content of this lesson together.

paragraphs: The first question was whether we couldn't call the model directly from where the data is. Snowflake AI functions (AI_COMPLETE, AI_FILTER, AI_AGG, AI_CLASSIFY) call models within SQL to analyze text and images row by row. AI_AGG aggregates datasets larger than the model's context window at once.

The Cortex Search service provides hybrid search combining vectors and keywords, including embedding and index update. Dynamic tables automatically update query results to match your target delay, so they can be used to keep AI function results up-to-date.

In summary, functional AI is suitable for conversion and classification of large quantities of rows, and search-as-a-service is suitable for semantic search and RAG at the query time. Both require permission to use, and their common advantage is that data is processed within an existing permissions framework rather than being moved out of the way.

In practice, the two methods are often combined into one flow. If you classify and summarize inquiries in a functional manner, the quality of service-type search filters and chatbot answers will both improve. Conversely, it is also possible to design a fragment found by search-as-a-service as input to a functional query.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Choose a method by first asking whether your task is to transform all rows or find the fragment that matches the query. You can then design permissions and renewal mechanisms.

glossary.def: This is a general-purpose AI function that generates a model’s response within SQL.
A function that aggregates multiple lines of text into one result according to a directive.
It is a managed hybrid search service that combines vectors and keywords.
This is a table that automatically updates query results according to the target delay.
This is the ability to call a model hosted by the platform as an API.

misconceptions.myth: To use an AI function, data must be sent externally.
misconceptions.fact: The documentation explains that the LLM provided is deployed within the Snowflake service boundary. No separate steps are required to take data out of the warehouse.

misconceptions.myth: AI function usage rights cannot be controlled separately.
misconceptions.fact: Administrators can revoke blanket privileges from PUBLIC and grant function-specific privileges to roles as needed. Since the role conditions for scalar and aggregate functions are different, check the requirements of the actual calling function.

misconceptions.myth: Search services have the same purpose as AI functions.
misconceptions.fact: Converting rows one by one is a functional type, and finding a document fragment that matches a query is a service type. The two can be used together, but they are not the same tool.

misconceptions.myth: AI functions always return the same result with the same input.
misconceptions.fact: The output of a generative model may vary from run to run. Classification functions with a set list of categories have stable results, but inputs with ambiguous boundaries can vary, so important results are saved and reused.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Snowflake AI functions call models within SQL to analyze text and images row by row.
AI_AGG aggregates datasets larger than the model context window at once.
The Cortex Search service provides hybrid search combining vectors and keywords, including embedding and index update.
Dynamic tables can be used to keep AI function results up-to-date by automatically updating query results to match the target delay (TARGET_LAG).
Functional AI is suitable for bulk row conversion and classification, and search-as-a-service is suitable for semantic search and RAG at the time of query, and requires permission to use.
